ideas.title: Evolvable reproductive recourse: sex-specific refractory delays and reserve banking as a mechanism linking genetic variance, mating ecology, and survival trade-offs
ideas.motivation: The original question asks what drives reproduction in living systems. Evidence from the subgraph shows that reproduction is driven by an interacting set of processes: heritable variance in reproductive timing supplies raw evolvability [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4416670776); assortative mating by timing can reshape genetic variance and adaptation under climate change [Author et al., 2021](https://openalex.org/W3141331266); sex-specific selection ties male fitness to mate attraction and female fitness to fertility-linked traits [Author et al., 2023](https://openalex.org/W4366817449); and reproduction-survival trade-offs generate sex-biased longevity [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4412678672). The unresolved bottleneck is not another single trait but a predictive, sex-aware, environmentally contingent mechanism that determines when reproductive strategies increase fitness and evolvability versus when they impose constraints. To address this, the idea imports state-dependent threshold and refractory-period decision rules from behavioral ecology/economic trade-off modelling [Author et al., 2016](https://openalex.org/W2554280009), temporal optimization under environmental variation from sex-allocation theory [Author et al., 1986](https://openalex.org/W2029353030), and lifecycle-stage partitioning of sexual selection and conflict [Author et al., 2019](https://openalex.org/W2989981305). The central mechanism is not an external optimizer but heritable variation in recourse capacity itself: individuals evolve cue thresholds, delay limits, reserve-banking efficiency, and refractory costs. The primary hypothesis is that a heritable structured recourse mechanism—conditional reproductive delay coupled with sex-specific reserve banking—causally maintains higher long-term fitness by preserving additive genetic variance in reproductive timing when cues are unreliable and mate or pollinator overlap is low. This is not ordinary plasticity or bet-hedging because the decision is cue- and state-dependent, stores reproductive potential for future use, creates temporal niche partitioning among genotypes, and evolves under explicit sex-specific survival and fertility constraints.
ideas.method_overview: This method is intended to solve the lack of a unified, sex-aware, environmentally contingent mechanism for reproductive drivers; it can be divided into 4 parts: (1) an evolvable recourse trait complex that controls conditional delay, refractory recovery, and reserve banking; (2) a stochastic ecological-mating kernel that generates cue reliability, temporal mate overlap, and pollinator or mate limitation; (3) a sex-specific lifecycle fitness ledger that separates pre-mating, mating, post-mating, and survival components; and (4) controlled evolutionary simulations and a common-garden microcosm test that first isolate the recourse effect and then explore boundary conditions.

proposed_method.name: Evolvable recourse trait complex
proposed_method.description: Represent recourse as a heritable mechanism, not an external optimizer. Individuals carry polygenic reaction norms for reproductive timing and for recourse parameters: cue threshold for reproduction, maximum conditional delay, refractory length, reserve conversion efficiency, cue-acquisition error, and sex-specific maintenance cost. The refractory/recovery state generalizes post-partum amenorrhea-like constraints, in which a reproductive event creates a temporary state that limits immediate future reproduction and couples current effort to future survival and fecundity [Author et al., 2016](https://openalex.org/W2554280009). Reserve banking stores deferred reproductive potential as female propagule or gamete reserves and male condition or mating-effort reserves, with decay and conversion rules. This creates temporal niche partitioning among genotypes and allows alleles to be expressed in later reproductive windows. The optimization template is a temporally varying sex-allocation problem, where the best allocation depends on environmental state and future expectations [Author et al., 1986](https://openalex.org/W2029353030). Because timing variance is heritable, the model can ask how recourse changes additive genetic variance and evolvability [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4416670776).

proposed_method.name: Stochastic ecological-mating kernel
proposed_method.description: Simulate fluctuating environmental optima for reproductive timing, imperfect cues, and mate or pollinator availability. Mating success depends on temporal overlap and assortative matching of reproductive timing, allowing nonrandom mating to inflate or depress genetic variance depending on environmental change [Author et al., 2021](https://openalex.org/W3141331266). Mate acquisition and attractive traits are sex-specific, so male fitness can depend more on flowering duration or display traits while female fitness depends more on fertility-linked traits, as observed in dioecious insect-pollinated plants [Author et al., 2023](https://openalex.org/W4366817449). The kernel can be parameterized for plants, animals, or digital organisms by changing the mapping from cue to mate availability and from display trait to mating success.

proposed_method.name: Sex-specific lifecycle fitness ledger
proposed_method.description: Partition fitness into lifecycle stages: survival to reproduction, mate acquisition, gamete transfer or fertilization, offspring production, and post-reproductive survival. This follows lifecycle-explicit approaches to sexual selection and sexual conflict, allowing genetic load and sexually antagonistic selection to be quantified rather than collapsed into a single fitness measure [Author et al., 2019](https://openalex.org/W2989981305). The ledger includes asymmetric trade-offs: female offspring production can constrain both sexes, whereas male mating effort can impose weaker indirect fertility constraints, producing sex-biased longevity under monogamy and other mating systems [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4412678672). - Trend Analysis: Trends:

Paper 0 to Paper 1:  
Paper 0 is best read as the 2021 modeling study, *Assortative mating can help adaptation of flowering time to a changing climate: Insights from a polygenic model*. It treats reproductive timing as a polygenic trait shaped by nonrandom mating. Its central advance is to show that assortative mating can have antagonistic effects on genetic variance: it creates positive associations among similar allelic effects, which can inflate genetic variance, but it can also reduce polymorphism, which depresses variance. Under environmental change, however, assortative mating can increase standing genetic variance, reduce the lag between the population and the moving optimum, and provide a fitness advantage relative to random mating. This connects directly to the seed idea that genetic variance in reproductive timing contributes to trait evolvability.  
Paper 1, the 2023 study *Sex-specific selection patterns in a dioecious insect-pollinated plant*, shifts the focus from abstract mating-system effects on genetic variance to the concrete phenotypic and sex-specific selection acting on reproductive traits. In *Silene dioica*, female fitness is more strongly associated with fertility-linked traits such as flower number and gamete production, while male fitness is shaped by flowering duration, corolla width, reproductive success, and number of mates. The transition therefore moves from “how mating patterns preserve or reshape genetic variation in reproductive timing” to “how that variation is translated into sex-specific reproductive success through natural selection, pollinator-mediated selection, and sexual selection.”

Paper 1 to Paper 2:  
Paper 1 emphasizes mate acquisition, floral trait selection, and sex-specific reproductive success. Paper 2, the 2025 study *Asymmetric life-history trade-offs shape sex-biased longevity patterns*, broadens the evolutionary frame from reproductive trait expression to the allocation trade-off between reproduction and survival. It models monogamous individuals evolving under sex-specific reproductive constraints: males trade survival against mating opportunities, while females trade survival against offspring production. The key result is that either sex can evolve greater longevity, but male-biased longevity evolves under a wider range of conditions because female longevity is more tightly constrained by offspring production, which affects the fertility of both sexes. The transition is therefore from “what traits determine mating and fertility success” to “how reproductive strategies shape survival, ageing, and lifespan evolution.” Reproduction is no longer treated only as a process of attracting mates or producing gametes; it becomes a central component of a broader life-history optimization problem.

Key Turning Points:

1. From random mating to nonrandom mating as an evolutionary mechanism.  
   The 2021 paper marks a turning point by treating assortative mating not merely as a demographic detail but as a mechanism that can alter genetic variance, adaptive tracking, and fitness under climate change. This moves the field beyond simple random-mating assumptions and connects reproductive timing directly to evolvability.

2. From general reproductive success to sex-specific selection.  
   The 2023 paper shifts attention from population-level mating dynamics to the different selective pressures experienced by males and females. Its use of Bateman-style metrics and trait-fitness associations shows that reproductive drivers are not sex-neutral. In males, mating success and attractive floral traits matter strongly; in females, fertility-linked traits are more central.

3. From trait selection to life-history trade-offs.  
   The 2025 paper expands the question from “which traits improve reproduction?” to “how does reproduction compete with survival?” This is a major conceptual shift because it places reproductive success inside a broader allocation framework where longevity, mortality, and sex-specific fertility constraints shape evolutionary outcomes.

4. From static adaptation to changing environments.  
   Across the subgraph, a key turning point is the movement from stable-optimum thinking toward environments that change directionally, fluctuate, or impose density-dependent mortality. The 2021 paper explicitly models climate change, while the 2025 paper introduces extrinsic mortality that can obscure evolved longevity differences. This makes the drivers of reproduction contingent on ecological context rather than fixed biological constants.

Recurring Limitations:

1. Strong context dependence.  
   The advantage of assortative mating depends on environmental change, stabilizing selection, and the extent to which genetic variance limits adaptation. The plant study finds limited pollinator-mediated selection under its experimental conditions, especially in the absence of pollen limitation. The longevity model shows that extrinsic mortality can obscure evolved sex-biased lifespan differences. In each case, the evolutionary outcome is highly conditional.

2. Simplified mating systems.  
   The 2021 model focuses on assortative mating by flowering time, the 2023 study focuses on a dioecious insect-pollinated plant, and the 2025 model assumes monogamy. These simplifications are useful, but they leave open how general the results are across polygamous systems, selfing species, hermaphrodites, animals with parental care, or systems with strong mate competition outside flowering overlap.

3. Incomplete integration of genetic variance, selection, and demography.  
   The 2021 paper emphasizes genetic variance and adaptation, the 2023 paper estimates selection on reproductive traits, and the 2025 paper models survival-reproduction trade-offs. However, none fully integrates all three levels: the maintenance of genetic variation, sex-specific trait selection, and life-history-demographic feedbacks in a single predictive framework.

4. Difficulty measuring reproductive trade-offs directly.  
   The papers recognize that reproduction is shaped by trade-offs, but the empirical and theoretical resolution of those trade-offs remains limited. For example, mating opportunity, gamete production, offspring production, survival, and longevity are difficult to measure simultaneously in natural populations, especially across changing environments.

[ABSTRACT] Competition for mate acquisition is the hallmark of any sexual organism. In insect-pollinated plants, competition to attract pollinators is expected to result in pollinator-mediated selection on attractive floral traits. This could overlap with sexual selection if the number of mating partners increases with pollinator attraction, resulting in an improved reproductive success. In this study, we measured a set of floral traits and estimated individual fitness in male and female Silene dioica in an experimental population. Results align with the predictions of Bateman's principles, in the absence of pollen limitation. In females, natural selection acted on traits that are typically linked with fertility (number of flowers and number of gametes), and selection strength was similar in open- and hand-pollinated females, suggesting a limited role of pollinator-mediated selection. In males, flowering duration and corolla width were positively associated with both reproductive success and number of mates, suggesting that sexual selection has played a role in the evolution of these traits. The use of Bateman's metrics further confirmed stronger sexual selection in males than in females. Taken together, our results shed light on the occurrence of sex-specific patterns of selection in an insect-pollinated plant population.

[ABSTRACT] Several empirical studies report fast evolutionary changes in flowering time in response to contemporary climate change. Flowering time is a polygenic trait under assortative mating, since flowering time of mates must overlap. Here, we test whether assortative mating, compared with random mating, can help better track a changing climate. For each mating pattern, our individual-based model simulates a population evolving in a climate characterized by stabilizing selection around an optimal flowering time, which can change directionally and/or fluctuate. We also derive new analytical predictions from a quantitative genetics model for the expected genetic variance at equilibrium, and its components, the lag of the population to the optimum and the population mean fitness. We compare these predictions between assortative and random mating, and to our simulation results. Assortative mating, compared with random mating, has antagonistic effects on genetic variance: it generates positive associations among similar allelic effects, which inflates the genetic variance, but it decreases genetic polymorphism, which depresses the genetic variance. In a stationary environment with substantial stabilizing selection, assortative mating affects little the genetic variance compared with random mating. In a changing climate, assortative mating however increases genetic variance compared to random mating, which diminishes the lag of the population to the optimum, and in most scenarios translates into a fitness advantage relative to random mating. The magnitude of this fitness advantage depends on the extent to which genetic variance limits adaptation, being larger for faster environmental changes and weaker stabilizing selection.

[ABSTRACT] Abstract Sex differences in ageing and lifespan are widespread across taxa, yet their evolutionary causes remain debated. A leading hypothesis suggests these differences are adaptive and driven by sex-specific life-history trade-offs, but formal theoretical support is lacking. To address this, we developed a mathematical model to investigate how such trade-offs shape lifespan evolution in a monogamous mating system. In the model, individuals evolve to optimise a trade-off between reproduction and survival – mediated by mating opportunities in males and offspring production in females. By systematically varying trade-off strengths, we show that either sex can evolve greater longevity, but male-biased longevity evolves under a broader set of conditions – consistent with patterns in monogamous species. This asymmetry arises because female longevity is more constrained: the trade-off between offspring production and survival directly affects the fertility of both sexes. In contrast, the male trade-off for mating opportunities has a weaker indirect effect on female fertility, allowing selection to more readily favour longer male lifespans. We also show that extrinsic density-dependent mortality can disproportionately affect the intrinsically longer-living sex, and obscure the magnitude of this evolved difference. Together, our results provide new theoretical insights into the adaptive bases of sex-biased longevity and highlight the importance of life-history trade-offs in shaping lifespan evolution.

ideas.title: Deferred reproductive capital: sex-specific invasion thresholds and sexually antagonistic cohort storage as drivers of reproductive evolvability
ideas.motivation: The original query asks what drives reproduction in living systems. In evolutionary ecology, a key answer is that heritable variation in reproductive timing shapes evolvability [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4416670776), nonrandom mating can alter genetic variance and adaptation under changing climates [Author et al., 2021](https://openalex.org/W3141331266), sex-specific selection assigns different fitness consequences to male and female reproductive traits [Author et al., 2023](https://openalex.org/W4366817449), and reproduction-survival trade-offs shape sex-biased longevity [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4412678672). However, these drivers remain separated: current work does not predict when a reproductive strategy increases fitness and evolvability versus when it becomes a constraint under unreliable phenological cues. The primary testable hypothesis is that a covariance-weighted deferred-capital threshold causally determines the invasion of sex-specific deferred recourse and, through sexually antagonistic cohort storage, the maintenance of additive genetic variance in reproductive timing. To avoid a same-field recombination, the idea imports elasticity-based resource valuation from economics [Author et al., 2013](https://openalex.org/W2036680378) and dynamic allocation optimization in temporally varying environments from economics [Author et al., 1986](https://openalex.org/W2029353030), then tests the resulting theory in a demogenetic individual-based framework from computational evolutionary modeling [Author et al., 2020](https://openalex.org/W3015117265).
ideas.method_overview: This method is intended to solve the lack of a predictive, sex-aware, environmentally contingent mechanism linking genetic variance in reproductive timing, mate acquisition, and survival trade-offs; it can be divided into 5 parts: (1) deferred reproductive capital state variables, (2) a sex-specific invasion inequality, (3) sexually antagonistic cohort storage genetics, (4) a demogenetic individual-based implementation, and (5) controlled hypothesis tests.

proposed_method.name: Deferred reproductive capital state and sex-specific conversion functions
proposed_method.description: Represent each individual as having sex-specific deferred reproductive capital K_s, refractory delay tau_s, decay rate delta_s, maintenance cost m_s, and survival cost lambda_s. At each reproductive bout, an individual divides available reproductive resources between immediate effort and K_s. Female K_s converts into future gamete or offspring production, while male K_s converts into future mate attraction, competition, or mating effort, reflecting sex-specific selection on fertility and mating success [Author et al., 2023](https://openalex.org/W4366817449). The survival cost of stored capital is coupled to reproduction-survival trade-offs and sex-biased longevity [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4412678672). Genetic variance in reproductive timing determines when stored capital can be deployed, linking the mechanism to trait evolvability [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4416670776).

proposed_method.name: Sex-specific invasion condition for deferred recourse
proposed_method.description: Derive an invasion condition for a rare deferred-capital modifier. Let q_t be a cue to immediate mating or pollination opportunity and F_s(tau_s) be future opportunity after the refractory delay. The expected marginal benefit of storing one unit of capital is B_s = eta_s * l_s(tau_s) * E_s[dW/dK_s] * Cov(q_t, F_s(tau_s)), where eta_s is conversion efficiency, l_s is refractory survival, and E_s[dW/dK_s] is a sex-specific fitness elasticity. The cost is C_s = m_s * tau_s + delta_s * tau_s + lost immediate reproduction + survival decrement. The modifier invades when the sex-weighted sum of B_s - C_s is positive. The elasticity term is borrowed from economics resource-elasticity theory [Author et al., 2013](https://openalex.org/W2036680378), and the cue-contingent allocation rule adapts economic optimization in temporally varying environments [Author et al., 1986](https://openalex.org/W2029353030).

proposed_method.name: Sexually antagonistic cohort storage
proposed_method.description: Add genetic architecture in which deferred-capital alleles have sex-limited or antagonistic pleiotropic effects: an allele that increases female reserve banking or refractory delay reduces male immediate mating effort, display, or flowering duration, and vice versa, because both sexes draw on a shared resource budget. This creates cohort storage: alleles can be expressed later through deferred capital and can be beneficial in one sex or temporal cohort while costly in another. This mechanism is designed to maintain additive genetic variance in reproductive timing beyond simple environmental buffering [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4416670776), to interact with assortative-mating effects on variance [Author et al., 2021](https://openalex.org/W3141331266), and to reflect sex-specific selection on reproductive traits [Author et al., 2023](https://openalex.org/W4366817449).

proposed_method.name: Demogenetic individual-based implementation
proposed_method.description: Implement the theory in an individual-based model that couples inheritance, demography, mate acquisition, fertility, survival, and environmental stochasticity, following demogenetic modeling approaches [Author et al., 2020](https://openalex.org/W3015117265). Individuals carry polygenic loci for reproductive timing [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4416670776), a deferred-capital modifier locus, and trait loci for sex-specific reproductive traits. Mating requires temporal overlap and can later include assortative mating by reproductive timing [Author et al., 2021](https://openalex.org/W3141331266). Reproduction reduces survival according to sex-specific trade-offs [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4412678672).

proposed_method.name: Controlled comparisons and observables
proposed_method.description: Define matched controls: immediate-only cue plasticity, fixed-delay, random-deferral, noncontingent reserve bank, sex-neutral deferred capital, and deferred capital without antagonistic pleiotropy. Observables include invasion frequency, additive genetic variance in reproductive timing, lag to environmental optimum, sex-specific lifetime reproductive success, longevity, and realized B_s/C_s. These controls separate information-based deferral from generic delay, storage, bet-hedging, and sex-specific mortality effects, while lag and variance metrics connect the mechanism to adaptation and evolvability [Author et al., 2021](https://openalex.org/W3141331266). Longevity and survival outputs connect it to life-history trade-offs [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4412678672).

analogy_mapping.inspiration: Resource Elasticity of Offspring Survival and the Optimal Evolution of Sex Ratios
analogy_mapping.concept: Elasticity of fitness outcomes to allocated resources
analogy_mapping.adaptation: The elasticity of future reproductive success to stored deferred capital becomes the sex-specific benefit term in the invasion condition, converting stored reproductive effort into a quantitative fitness return.

analogy_mapping.inspiration: An optimisation principle for sex allocation in a temporally varying environment
analogy_mapping.concept: Fitness-maximizing allocation under temporal environmental variation
analogy_mapping.adaptation: The cue-contingent decision to invest immediately versus defer reproductive capital is treated as a temporally contingent optimization policy with a testable threshold.

analogy_mapping.inspiration: A demogenetic individual based model for the evolution of traits and genome architecture under sexual selection
analogy_mapping.concept: Demogenetic individual-based modeling that couples demography, inheritance, trait evolution, and mating dynamics
analogy_mapping.adaptation: This modeling scaffold is used to simulate polygenic reproductive timing, deferred capital, sex-specific selection, mate overlap, and survival trade-offs in replicated populations.

experiment_plan: Derive the rare-modifier invasion condition in a simplified analytical model with fixed demography and a single deferred-capital locus; compute B_s/C_s from cue-future covariance, conversion efficiency, refractory survival, maintenance, decay, and lost immediate reproduction.

Build the baseline demogenetic simulation with polygenic reproductive timing, environmental stochasticity, temporal mate overlap, fertility, and survival; hold population size, mutation rate, resource acquisition, and mating kernel fixed in the primary phase [Author et al., 2020](https://openalex.org/W3015117265).

Primary one-factor test: vary only the deferred-capital benefit-cost ratio B/C by changing cue-future covariance while holding all costs, delays, conversion efficiencies, genetic architecture, and demography fixed; introduce a structured sex-specific deferred-capital allele at 1 percent frequency into immediate-only populations.
Run the active control at the same B/C levels: an immediate-only cue-plastic genotype that uses the cue but cannot store capital; this isolates the effect of deferred capital from cue responsiveness.

At B/C below, at, and above threshold, run confound controls: fixed-delay with the same mean delay, random-deferral with the same mean deferral probability, noncontingent reserve bank with the same mean stored capital, unstructured population mixture of immediate and fixed-delay individuals, sex-neutral deferred capital, and deferred capital without sexually antagonistic pleiotropy.

Measure invasion as deferred-capital allele frequency change over 200 generations, additive genetic variance in reproductive timing, mean fitness, and lag to optimum; prediction: deferred capital invades and raises variance only when B/C is greater than 1, while immediate-only, fixed-delay, random-deferral, and noncontingent bank do not show the same threshold response.

Rule out trivial confounders by logging realized cue-outcome covariance, maintenance and decay costs, survival, mating success, fertility, and resource budgets; if fixed-delay, random-deferral, or noncontingent bank matches deferred capital, reject the information-based mechanism; if sex-neutral deferred capital matches sex-specific deferred capital, reject the sex-specific constraint mechanism; if neutral markers drift similarly, attribute variance changes cautiously.

Test sexually antagonistic cohort storage directly by comparing deferred capital with antagonistic pleiotropy to deferred capital without antagonism under identical B/C; prediction: antagonistic storage maintains higher additive genetic variance and stable polymorphism over 1000 generations.

After the core hypothesis is confirmed, vary secondary factors one at a time: assortative mating strength, directional environmental change, fluctuating selection, density-dependent mortality, and mating-system structure; record boundary conditions where deferred capital helps or constrains adaptation [Author et al., 2021](https://openalex.org/W3141331266), [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4412678672).

Translate to an empirical pilot: choose a short-lived dioecious plant or insect with measurable delayed reproductive structures or skipped mating bouts, manipulate only cue reliability of mates or pollinators, keep resource levels fixed, and track deferred-capital proxies, sex-specific fitness, survival, and allele frequency; use immediate-only, fixed-delay, and random-deferral line controls [Author et al., 2023](https://openalex.org/W4366817449).
